metadata.title: Universal Reviewer Knowledge Pack
metadata.description: Shared reviewer knowledge for narrative interpretation, speaker/target/victim reasoning, quotation handling, context handling, and confidence calibration.

pack.title: Universal Reviewer Knowledge Pack
pack.purpose: Provide reasoning knowledge that applies to every GCAM subject before subject-specific packs are consulted.
required_evidence: The exact local chunk should be read for speaker cues, quotation marks, dialogue markers, narration markers, and scene framing.
The reviewer should preserve the literal wording before inferring who is speaking, who is being addressed, and what role each participant has in the scene.
When the text contains a quoted or reported line, the reviewer must distinguish the quoted speaker from the narrator or reporter.
When evidence is mixed or ambiguous, the reviewer should preserve the conflict rather than force a confident classification.
insufficient_evidence: A guess about speaker, listener, target, or victim that is not anchored to the local chunk.
A single narrative cue that is overridden by a stronger counter-cue in the same scene.
A claim that the scene is a dream, flashback, satire, or documentary without supporting textual signals.
A confidence value that is inflated beyond what the actual narrative cues support.
reviewer_heuristics: Decide whether the content is dialogue, narration, or scene description before deciding what it means.
Separate the speaker from the narrator whenever the text contains quotation, reported speech, or multi-speaker conversation.
Identify the listener only when the text actually addresses someone or the reply structure makes the listener visible.
Identify the target and victim only after checking whether the line is praise, criticism, condemnation, threat, joke, or neutral reference.
Use the surrounding scene to distinguish protagonist speech from antagonist speech without assuming either one is inherently true.
Treat educational, documentary, historical, and role-play framing as context that can change interpretation.
Treat irony, satire, metaphor, and symbolic language as meaning-shifting devices, not literal assertions.
When the story contains hallucinations, dreams, or flashbacks, preserve the timeline and do not confuse the inner scene with present reality.
Use conflicting evidence to lower confidence instead of resolving the conflict by invention.
Calibrate confidence to the clarity of the local evidence, not to the intensity of the wording.
positive_examples: Dialogue marker: A: "أنا لا أوافق" — clear dialogue with a visible speaker.
Reported speech: قال الراوي إن الشاهد ذكر العبارة — the narrator reports another speaker's words.
Victim reasoning: الشخصية تقول إنه تأذى — the text explicitly supports a victim role.
Multi-speaker scene: A يرد، ثم B يعترض — the conversation has multiple speakers.
Condemnation: القصة تدين الفعل وتصفه بالخطأ — the scene rejects the content instead of endorsing it.
Documentary frame: الوثائقي يشرح الحدث — the scene is informational rather than endorsing.
Historical frame: يتحدث عن الماضي بوصفه حدثًا تاريخيًا — the text frames the content as history.
Conflicting evidence: يظهر المدح ثم يأتي التصحيح — the reviewer must preserve the conflict and reduce confidence.
negative_examples: Treating every quoted line as narration — quotation can change the speaker.
Assuming the listener is always the nearest named person — that can misread indirect address.
Equating villain dialogue with authorial endorsement — the speaker role matters.
Calling a documentary example a present-tense assertion — the frame matters.
Treating metaphor as literal proof — figurative language should not be over-literalized.
Forcing a high-confidence role assignment when the text is ambiguous.
Using off-chunk memory as if it were literal evidence.
Declaring a scene a flashback or dream without any explicit cue.
common_false_positives: Quoted speech mistaken for narrator speech.
Indirect speech mistaken for direct speech.
A listener inferred from context when the text never addresses anyone.
A victim inferred from emotional tone without textual support.
A role-play or fictional scene misread as a real-world statement.
A joke, irony, or satire line misread as a literal claim.
A metaphor or symbol misread as an actual event.
Overconfident interpretation of a multi-speaker disagreement.
reporting_guidance: Describe the narrative frame first, then the speaker, then the listener or target, then the likely meaning.
Use exact wording for quoted or reported speech and explicitly say when the line is being reported rather than asserted.
If context is unclear, report the ambiguity and lower confidence rather than forcing an interpretation.
Keep the universal reasoning layer separate from subject-specific legal analysis.
When the scene is educational, historical, documentary, fictional, or satirical, call that out clearly because it affects interpretation.
When multiple interpretations remain plausible, mention the strongest one and the unresolved alternative.
